title: Who Regulates the Room
bigQuestion: When people train or compete in a combat sport, who makes the safety rules, and who answers when someone gets hurt?

story.title: A License by the Door
story.kicker: A framed state license hangs in a Chicago boxing gym, but it does not cover the room itself.
paragraphs: A boxing gym sits above a tire shop on Chicago's Southwest Side. A framed paper hangs beside its front door. It is a state license from the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. It says the owner, Mr. Reyes, may work as a second, the helper in a boxer's corner on fight night.

A high school junior named Aaliyah comes in to sign up. Her mother reads the license and asks a question. "So the state checked this gym?" Mr. Reyes shakes his head. The license covers him at a professional bout, he explains. The room itself only needs a city business license and a fire inspection.

Aaliyah wrestles for her school, too. Her team follows other rules. There are weigh-ins before each meet, and a referee checks every wrestler's skin. Last year a teammate hit her head and had to sit out. A form from a doctor was needed before she could return.

Aaliyah's mother takes a photo of the license. On the drive home, they count the rule makers they saw in one afternoon. There was the state, the city, the school, a doctor and a national rule book for high school wrestling. Each one watches a different part of the same sport.
story.think: Why might a state license the people at a professional bout but not the gym where they train?

lessons.title: Bare Knuckles and Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s, boxing moved from outlawed bare-knuckle fights to gloved bouts under the Queensberry Rules.
reading: Older English boxing followed the *London Prize Ring Rules*, first written in 1838 and revised in 1853. Fighters used bare fists. A round ended only when a man went down, so fights could last hours. Most American states treated these fights as illegal. Promoters often held them in secret places to avoid the police.

In 1867 a new code was published in London. John Graham Chambers wrote it, and John Sholto Douglas, the ninth Marquess of Queensberry, lent his name. The *Queensberry Rules* required padded gloves and three-minute rounds with one minute of rest. A fighter who was down had ten seconds to rise. The code made boxing look more like a sport with a clock.

The change reached the heavyweight title in two famous fights. On July 8, 1889, John L. Sullivan beat Jake Kilrain in 75 rounds at Richburg, Mississippi. It was the last heavyweight title fight under bare-knuckle rules, and Sullivan was later prosecuted in Mississippi for taking part. On September 7, 1892, James J. Corbett beat Sullivan in New Orleans, wearing gloves under Queensberry rules.

the boxing code published in 1867 that required gloves and three-minute rounds
a person or company that organizes and sells tickets to a bout

lessons.title: New York Tries Three Laws
lessons.mainIdea: New York legalized boxing, banned it and legalized it again before the 1920 Walker Law made the change last.
reading: New York was the biggest boxing market in the United States. It also changed its mind several times. In 1896 the *Horton Law* allowed boxing matches run by athletic clubs. Critics said the bouts were brutal and tied to gambling. In 1900 the state repealed the law, and prize fighting was banned again.

In 1911 the *Frawley Law* opened the door partway. It allowed bouts of up to ten rounds. It also set up a state commission to watch over boxing. Official decisions were not allowed, so a bout ended with no winner declared. Newspaper writers often named the winner instead. The Frawley Law was repealed in 1917.

In 1920 the state passed the Walker Law. It legalized boxing with judges' decisions and bouts of up to fifteen rounds. It also created the New York State Athletic Commission. This time the law lasted. The three laws show how a state can test a new rule, reverse it and then try again with stronger supervision.

words.d: a New York law of 1896 that allowed club boxing; repealed in 1900
a New York law of 1911 that allowed ten-round bouts with no official decision; repealed in 1917
to cancel a law officially

check.why: Critics of brutality and gambling won repeal of the Horton Law in 1900.

check.why: The Walker Law of 1920 legalized decisions and created the lasting state commission.

lessons.title: What the Walker Law Built
lessons.mainIdea: The Walker Law made boxing a licensed trade, and other states, including Illinois, built similar systems.
reading: The Walker Law was named for state senator James J. Walker. He later served as mayor of New York City, starting in 1926. His law made boxing a *licensed* business. Boxers, managers, seconds, referees, judges and promoters all needed a license from the new *athletic commission*. The commission could suspend a license or hold back a purse.

The commission also required medical checks before bouts. A doctor had to examine each boxer. The commission set the number of rounds and approved each card of bouts. In this way, a state agency began watching the room on fight night. Other states soon set up their own commissions on the New York model.

Illinois legalized professional boxing in the 1920s. On September 22, 1927, Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey fought at Soldier Field in Chicago before more than 100,000 people. Today the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation licenses professional boxers and officials. It works under the state's Boxing and Full-contact Martial Arts Act.

words.d: a government agency that licenses boxers and officials and supervises bouts
holding official permission from the government to do a job
the money paid to boxers for a bout

lessons.title: Fifteen Rounds Become Twelve
lessons.mainIdea: After Duk Koo Kim died following a 1982 title fight, major boxing organizations shortened championship bouts to twelve rounds.
reading: On November 13, 1982, Ray Mancini defended his lightweight title against Duk Koo Kim of South Korea. The bout took place outside Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, Nevada. It was scheduled for fifteen rounds. Kim was stopped in the fourteenth round and fell into a coma. He died four days later.

Professional titles are awarded by *sanctioning bodies*, private groups that rank boxers and approve title fights. The World Boxing Council, or WBC, was the first to act. Soon after Kim's death, it cut its title bouts from fifteen rounds to twelve. The World Boxing Association and the International Boxing Federation later made the same change.

The fight led to other changes too. Commissions paid more attention to medical exams before and after bouts. Kim's death also touched people far from the ring. His mother died by suicide a few months later, and the referee, Richard Green, died the next year. The story shows how one death can reshape a rule book.

words.d: a private organization that ranks boxers and approves championship fights, such as the WBC
a fight for a title, once scheduled for fifteen rounds and now for twelve
the World Boxing Council, a sanctioning body founded in 1963

check.why: The WBC shortened championship bouts to twelve rounds, and other bodies later followed.

lessons.title: Congress Steps Into Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: In 1996 and 2000, Congress passed laws that set national floors for boxer safety and fair contracts.
reading: For most of the 1900s, only states regulated boxing. Rules varied from one state to the next. A boxer suspended in one state could sometimes fight in another. Promoters could move bouts to places with weak commissions or none at all. Reformers asked Congress to set a national floor.

Congress passed the *Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996*. It said no professional bout may be held in the United States unless a state or tribal commission supervises it. It required a physical exam for each boxer and an ambulance and doctor at each bout. It also created a national identification card for professional boxers.

In 2000 Congress passed the *Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act*. Ali, the former heavyweight champion, lent his name to the effort. The law aimed to protect boxers from unfair contracts. It also required sanctioning bodies to make their ranking rules public. State and tribal commissions work together through the Association of Boxing Commissions.

words.d: a federal law requiring commission supervision, physicals and medical staff at pro boxing bouts
a federal law of 2000 that aimed to protect boxers from unfair contracts and hidden rankings
an athletic commission run by a Native American nation, which can supervise bouts on its lands

choices: that every bout be held in New York

check.why: The 1996 law banned pro bouts in the U.S. without commission supervision.

check.q: What was one goal of the Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act of 2000?
choices: to make sanctioning bodies publish their ranking rules
check.why: The Ali Act required ranking rules to be public and aimed to protect boxers from unfair contracts.

check.q: Why did reformers want a federal boxing law?
choices: State rules varied, and bouts could move to places with weak commissions.
check.why: Uneven state rules let promoters and suspended boxers move to places with little oversight.

lessons.title: Who Governs Olympic Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic boxing answers to an international federation, and in the 2020s the IOC replaced the old federation with a new one.
reading: Olympic boxing is amateur boxing. It follows different rules and bodies than professional bouts. Boxing first appeared at the Olympics at St. Louis in 1904. The *International Amateur Boxing Association*, known as AIBA, was founded in 1946 to govern the amateur sport worldwide. In the United States, USA Boxing is the national governing body.

Women's boxing was added to the Olympics at London in 2012. The American Claressa Shields won the middleweight gold there and again in 2016. That first women's event came 108 years after men's Olympic boxing began. Women had fought in amateur tournaments long before the Olympics allowed them.

AIBA faced years of problems with judging, money and leadership. In 2019 the International Olympic Committee suspended its recognition. The IOC ran the boxing events itself at Tokyo 2020, held in 2021, and at Paris 2024. AIBA had renamed itself the IBA, and in 2023 the IOC withdrew recognition. A new federation, *World Boxing*, was founded in 2023 to take its place.

words.d: AIBA, founded in 1946 to govern amateur boxing; later renamed IBA
an international federation founded in 2023 to govern Olympic boxing
the organization that runs one Olympic sport in one country, such as USA Boxing

check.why: Boxing debuted at the 1904 Olympics in St. Louis.

check.q: What did the IOC do in 2019?
check.why: After problems with judging, money and leadership, the IOC suspended AIBA in 2019.

check.q: Which federation was founded in 2023 to govern Olympic boxing?
check.why: World Boxing was founded in 2023 after the IOC withdrew recognition from the IBA.

lessons.title: The Lystedt Law
lessons.mainIdea: Washington's 2009 Lystedt Law was the first state law requiring a young athlete with a suspected concussion to leave play until cleared.
reading: In October 2006, Zackery Lystedt was a 13-year-old football player in Maple Valley, Washington. He hit his head during a middle school game. He went back in after a short rest. After the game he collapsed from a brain injury. He survived after emergency surgery but faced a long recovery.

A *concussion* is a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head or body. It can happen in football, soccer, wrestling, judo or boxing. Doctors warn that a second blow before healing can cause much worse harm. Lystedt's family, doctors and lawyers pushed Washington lawmakers to act.

In May 2009 Governor Christine Gregoire signed the *Lystedt Law*. It had three main parts. Athletes and parents had to sign a concussion information sheet each year. An athlete with a suspected concussion had to be removed from play. Return required written clearance from a licensed health care provider trained in concussions.

words.d: a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head or body
Washington's 2009 youth concussion law, named for Zackery Lystedt
written permission from a health care provider to return to play

lessons.title: Illinois Concussion Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois passed a youth concussion law in 2011 and expanded it in 2015 to cover returning to class as well as to play.
reading: After Washington acted, other states followed quickly. Oregon passed Max's Law in 2009, named for high school football player Max Conradt. By 2014 every state had some kind of youth concussion law. Most copied Washington's three parts: education, removal from play and written clearance.

Illinois passed its law in 2011. It required school boards to adopt concussion policies that match the rules of the Illinois High School Association. A student athlete with a suspected concussion must be removed from practice or play. The student may not return without clearance from a doctor or trained athletic trainer. The IHSA also wrote its own return-to-play policy for all its sports.

In 2015 Illinois expanded the rules with the Youth Sports Concussion Safety Act. Each school must have a *concussion oversight team* that writes a *return-to-learn* plan as well as a return-to-play plan. Return-to-learn means a student may need lighter schoolwork while the brain heals. Coaches and officials must complete concussion training.

words.d: a group at each Illinois school that sets plans for students recovering from concussions
a plan that eases a student back into schoolwork after a concussion
a licensed health professional who cares for athletes' injuries

lessons.title: Weigh-ins and Skin Checks
lessons.mainIdea: After three college wrestlers died cutting weight in 1997, wrestling rule makers added weight programs and kept skin checks at weigh-ins.
reading: Wrestlers compete in *weight classes*, so a match pairs people of similar size. For decades, some wrestlers tried to lose weight fast before a weigh-in. In late 1997, three college wrestlers died within about six weeks while trying to lose weight quickly. They wrestled in North Carolina, Wisconsin and Michigan.

The NCAA changed its rules in 1998. It moved weigh-ins closer to the start of competition. It banned rubber suits and saunas for losing weight. It also set up a weight certification program early in each season. High school rule makers soon took similar steps.

The *NFHS*, the National Federation of State High School Associations, writes the national high school wrestling rules. It was founded in Chicago in 1920. Its rules require each state to run a weight management program. That program sets a lowest allowed weight for each wrestler and limits how fast a wrestler may drop to it. At weigh-ins, officials also check skin for contagious conditions. A wrestler with a sore needs a doctor's signed form to compete.

the National Federation of State High School Associations, founded in Chicago in 1920; it writes high school rule books
a required plan that sets each high school wrestler's lowest allowed weight
an official's look at wrestlers' skin at weigh-ins to stop contagious infections from spreading

lessons.title: A Studio Needs No State License
lessons.mainIdea: In most U.S. states, a martial arts studio can open without any state license to teach, so private groups set its standards.
reading: States license many jobs that touch the public. Illinois licenses barbers, nurses, electricians and professional boxing officials. In most states, though, no license is needed to teach karate, judo or taekwondo. A studio usually needs a city business license, a lease and a building that passes fire and safety codes.

Standards inside a studio come from *private* groups instead. The Kodokan in Tokyo, founded in 1882, awards judo ranks. The Kukkiwon in Seoul, opened in 1972, issues taekwondo rank certificates. National bodies such as USA Judo certify coaches and referees. A studio may join these groups, but in most places the law does not require it.

This gap matters for families. A certificate on the wall shows that a private group approved a teacher's rank. It does not show that a state checked the room or the teacher. Parents can ask whether a studio belongs to a national body, carries insurance and runs background checks. Those questions help families learn who stands behind the sign.

words.d: government permission needed to work in certain jobs, such as barber or boxing referee
run by people or groups, not by the government
an official approval from a group, such as a coaching or rank certificate

lessons.title: The Sports Act and National Bodies
lessons.mainIdea: The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport, and those bodies set rules for their member clubs.
reading: In the 1970s, U.S. amateur sport was split among rival groups. The Amateur Athletic Union and college groups often fought over who could send athletes to international events. In 1975 President Gerald Ford created the President's Commission on Olympic Sports to study the problem. Its report led to a new federal law.

Congress passed the *Amateur Sports Act of 1978*. It made the U.S. Olympic Committee the coordinating body for Olympic sport. It let the committee recognize one national governing body for each sport. The law also protected athletes' right to compete. In 1998 Congress renamed it the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

Today USA Judo, USA Taekwondo, USA Wrestling and USA Boxing are the national governing bodies for their sports. They register member clubs, certify coaches and referees and run national championships. Adults in these clubs must follow SafeSport rules. A club that joins a governing body accepts a rule book that reaches from the national office into its own room.

words.d: a federal law that organized U.S. Olympic sport under one national governing body per sport
a U.S. sports organization founded in 1888 that once controlled many amateur sports
a local club that registers with a national governing body and follows its rules
